text: A biopsy is usually unnecessary when the clinical picture and imaging are typical; it is kept for unusual or uncertain cases, or when a malignant change is suspected.
Every suspected bone lesion should undergo biopsy so that the diagnosis can be confirmed histologically before anything else is done.
To learn how much of the skeleton is involved, patients aged five years and older should have whole-body bone scintigraphy.
Imaging plays an important role in assessing the disease and its complications.
Histology can mislead: a sample may look like another lesion or come back falsely negative, and repeat sampling may then be needed.
When the diagnosis is uncertain, especially with a single isolated lesion, testing for a GNAS variant is recommended.
Because the mutation is present only in the affected bone, a blood sample often misses it; a negative result from blood does not exclude the disease, while lesional tissue is more informative.
For lesions of the skull and face, thin-slice computed tomography is the key imaging study.
Lesions that cause no symptoms or problems can simply be watched over time instead of being operated on, and this applies to children as well.
In children, all lesions should be removed surgically as early as possible to prevent deformity.

In typical cases no biopsy is needed. When the diagnosis is uncertain, particularly for a single lesion, a GNAS variant test is recommended. Thin-slice CT is the main study when the skull is involved.
From the age of five, a whole-body bone scan shows the extent of skeletal disease. Lesions without symptoms can be observed rather than operated on.
Fibrous dysplasia is caused by activating GNAS mutations that raise cAMP levels in bone-forming cells, which leads to fibro-osseous tissue.
Blood is the preferred sample for GNAS testing, and a negative blood result reliably excludes fibrous dysplasia.
